faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth, one star periodically passes in front of the other. Each eclipse dims the combined light we receive. By measuring these periodic dips in brightness, we can infer the orbital period, the relative sizes of the stars, and other key properties without needing a telescope pointed at the system.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: A candidate is a star that has passed the early vetting stages - statistical checks and novelty cross-matching - and shows a signal consistent with an eclipsing binary. A 'confirmed' result on Star Vetter specifically means the candidate has passed the automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the signal originates from the target star itself and not from a nearby contaminant. Confirmation here does not mean the result has been independently verified by another team or published in the scientific literature.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and 'confirmed' result?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a machine learning model (histogram gradient boosting) trained on 1533 labeled examples to assign a score to each candidate. This score is a second opinion on the quality of the signal. It was trained to outperform a baseline rule that rejects most false positives but at the cost of high false-alarm rate. However, the ML score itself does not currently gate which candidates get checked or make any decisions in the pipeline - it provides additional context only.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score, and what does it do?

faqs.answer: Each candidate undergoes a fully automated pixel-level check that inspects the spatial distribution of the signal in the TESS imaging data. This check confirms whether the brightness variations originate from the target star or from a nearby object whose light blends into the target's aperture. Candidates that pass this automated check are listed as 'confirmed' on the site.
faqs.question: How are candidates checked for false alarms?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a check that compares the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If the two sets of eclipses have significantly different depths, it suggests the measured period may be an alias of the true period. When this occurs, candidates are flagged with information about the period ambiguity on their individual pages.
faqs.question: What happens if the orbital period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate on this site includes a direct link to its light curve in the TESS archive, along with orbital period and eclipse depth measurements derived from that light curve. You can download the data and inspect it using publicly available tools to form your own assessment.
faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate result myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter's confirmed candidates page is the end point of this automated pipeline. The site does not conduct spectroscopic follow-up, coordinate observations with other telescopes, add results to official catalogs, or track what happens afterward. What researchers or survey projects do with these candidates is outside the scope of this project.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after Star Vetter lists it?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from the TESS satellite. The pipeline samples stars from TESS target lists, extracts light curves, applies statistical vetting to reject noise and instrumental artifacts, cross-checks results against six known variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and then runs a fully automated pixel-level check to confirm that the signal comes from the target star rather than a nearby object. So far, 156 candidates have passed this pixel-level check across 1.2% of the available sky. The results are trustworthy because the pipeline combines multiple independent filters - statistical gates, catalog cross-matching, and automated pixel inspection - and because every confirmed candidate carries transparent information about its light curve properties. That said, candidates may carry individual caveats noted on their pages, and confirmation by this pipeline is distinct from spectroscopic follow-up or scientific verification by other teams.
